summary: PRANA (Physiological Readiness & Autonomy Network for Astronauts) is an offline-first health app that lets astronauts gather, evaluate and act on their own health indicators, even when a reply from Earth takes 40 minutes. A guided 5-minute daily check walks the astronaut through each measurement with simple instructions: blood pressure, heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood, stress and symptoms, plus a playable reaction-time test (fatigue) and an Amsler vision grid (SANS eye changes). PRANA compares every reading with NASA/clinical safety limits and with the astronaut’s own pre-flight normal, and rolls 18 indicators into one Readiness score and NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. Each finding is explained in plain language and turned into action: a daily countermeasure plan, a symptom guide with danger-sign checks and treatment steps, live NASA DONKI solar-storm alerts, and delay-aware messaging to the flight surgeon in which the astronaut controls what is shared. We validated the personal-baseline method on real Inspiration4 crew blood data from NASA OSDR. It found post-landing changes that standard lab ranges miss. PRANA matters because on Mars, astronauts must be their own first doctor.
details:
Project Details

What it does. On long missions, astronauts face five hazards mapped by NASA’s Human Research Program: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. These bring bone loss, heart deconditioning, eye changes (SANS), immune changes, poor sleep and low mood. On the way to Mars the signal delay reaches 22 minutes each way, so the crew must spot and handle these changes themselves. PRANA is an on-board health companion built for that. It follows a simple loop: Gather → Evaluate → Act.

1. Gather. A guided daily check (6 steps, about 5 minutes) asks for each measurement and shows how to take it, because the challenge reminds us not to assume astronauts are experts at assessing themselves. It covers blood pressure, resting heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, fasting blood sugar, sleep hours, mood, stress and symptoms. It also includes two real interactive tests. One is a Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) for fatigue, a standard measure in spaceflight research. The other is an Amsler grid for early signs of SANS. Sensor values (wearable, dosimeter, cabin CO₂) pre-fill the form, and the astronaut confirms or corrects them. Eighteen indicators are tracked in total.

2. Evaluate. An explainable engine checks every indicator in three layers: (a) NASA-STD-3001 and clinical safety limits; (b) the astronaut’s personal baseline (pre-flight mean ± 2 SD), because astronauts are outliers and population ranges hide meaningful drift; (c) a 14-day trend for early warning. Results roll up into one Readiness score and the five NASA hazards, shown with colour coding, charts, and a clickable body map (brain, eyes, heart, lungs, bones, muscles, immune system, metabolism). Every flag answers “Why am I seeing this?” with the value, the person’s normal, the deviation and the NASA reference.

3. Act. Every finding links to concrete countermeasures with three escalation levels: do it yourself → involve the Crew Medical Officer → consult Earth. A symptom guide covers nine common spaceflight complaints (motion sickness, headache, back pain, congestion, insomnia, rash, eye irritation, fever, low mood). It checks danger signs first, then gives self-care steps, medical-kit use and when to recheck. The radiation page tracks dose against the 600 mSv career limit, shows live NASA DONKI space-weather alerts and the storm-shelter protocol, and charts cabin CO₂. The Earth link simulates real light-time delay (Moon 1.3 s, Mars 3–22 min). The astronaut chooses which data categories are shared, which addresses the known problem of crew under-reporting symptoms. Routine prompts, XP, streaks and badges reward self-care rather than “good numbers”.

Validation on real data. We applied the personal-baseline method to the real blood panel of the four SpaceX Inspiration4 crew (NASA OSDR, OSD-575). The day after landing it found 5 changes that sit outside each person’s own normal but inside the lab’s reference range, so a standard report would not show them. Blood sugar rose an average of 24% against each person’s own baseline, yet only one reading was outside the lab range. The data also shows why PRANA asks for a retest before acting: three crew had implausibly low glucose at R+45 at the same time without symptoms, which points to sample handling rather than illness. (n = 4 on a 3-day flight; we use it to show the method, not to make clinical claims.)

Benefits and impact. Earth-independent self-care for Moon and Mars crews; early detection before limits are crossed; less load on flight surgeons; and astronaut-owned data that builds trust. The same tool can serve Antarctic stations, submarines, offshore crews and remote clinics.

How it’s built. React + TypeScript + Vite; UI built with Untitled UI React (Tailwind CSS v4 + React Aria, open source); Recharts. It runs 100% in the browser with no server, works offline, and keeps data in local storage on the device. Four mission profiles (ISS, Lunar base, Mars transit, Mars base) change gravity, radiation dose rate (from published MSL-RAD, Curiosity RAD and Chang’e-4 measurements) and comms delay. A 180-day simulated mission with four fictional crew members demonstrates scenarios: a CO₂ scrubber fault, a solar particle event, viral reactivation, missed exercise, isolation and sleep loss, and SANS.

Creativity. Personal baselines instead of population thresholds; real in-app clinical tests; a symptom guide that puts danger signs first; delay-aware messaging with privacy controls; live NASA space-weather data; and validation on real astronaut data.

Factors we considered. Explainability over black-box AI (a crew must trust the advice); offline operation; low cognitive load and simple instructions; privacy and fear of being grounded; honest labelling of simulated vs real data; and that PRANA is decision support, not a medical device. Thresholds and treatments would need flight-surgeon validation.
